lessons.title: The Nature of God and the Shekhinah

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the Shema?
A) A Jewish prayer for the dead
B) The central Jewish declaration of God's oneness, from Deuteronomy 6:4
C) A set of dietary laws from the Torah
D) The Jewish calendar for festivals
practice_questions.marks: B) The central Jewish declaration of God's oneness, from Deuteronomy 6:4 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Hebrew term for the divine presence in Judaism.
practice_questions.marks: Shekhinah [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two attributes of God in Jewish teaching.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct attribute, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: God as One / monotheism; God as Creator; God as Law-Giver; God as Judge; God as loving and merciful (chesed); God as present (Shekhinah).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the belief that God is both Just and Merciful influences Jewish life.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons, both with clear explanation and development ('because...', 'this means that...'). At least one named source cited and developed (e.g. Deuteronomy 6:4 / Shema; Genesis 1:1; the Rosh Hashanah / Yom Kippur liturgy; Maimonides' Thirteen Principles). Both attributes of justice and mercy addressed, with sub-tradition contrast a bonus (e.g. Orthodox emphasis on strict observance; Reform emphasis on mercy and intention). Secure: Both attributes addressed, source present but not fully developed. Developing: One attribute developed, source named but not linked to the point. Emerging: Basic points, little development, no source.

practice_questions.text:
'The most important teaching in Judaism is that God is One.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Jewish teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is recited twice daily and at the point of death — its centrality signals that monotheism is the foundation of all Jewish belief and practice. Maimonides lists the oneness of God as the second of his Thirteen Principles, after only God's existence. All other Jewish teachings — the covenant, the mitzvot, prayer — rest on the premise that there is one God. Arguments against: Some Jewish thinkers and communities emphasise that Judaism is fundamentally a way of life rather than a set of beliefs; observing the mitzvot (practical commandments) may be more central than any creedal statement. Others might argue that the covenant with Abraham or Moses is more foundational because it establishes the special relationship between God and the Jewish people — not merely who God is, but how God acts in history. Non-religious perspectives: A humanist might argue that ethical teachings (justice, tzedakah, Pikuach Nefesh) are more important than any theological claim, since they produce measurable good in the world. Justified conclusion required: e.g. 'The oneness of God is the most important teaching because without it every other belief loses its foundation, although the covenant and the mitzvot show how that oneness is expressed in lived Jewish experience.' Mastering: Balanced, developed arguments for and against; religious sources cited on both sides; justified conclusion present. Secure: Arguments on both sides, source cited, conclusion present but not fully reasoned. Developing: One-sided or limited development; conclusion absent or weak. Emerging: Basic points, listing, no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Rachel is a 16-year-old student attending a Reform synagogue in Leeds. Her rabbi explains that the Shekhinah is present whenever Jews study Torah together. Explain two reasons why the concept of the Shekhinah might be important to Rachel and her community.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark per reason identified, 1 mark for each reason developed. Example answers: The Shekhinah offers comfort — it teaches that God is not distant but present with the community, especially during times of difficulty (e.g. when studying or praying together after a period of loss). The Shekhinah encourages communal worship and Torah study — knowing that God's presence is found where Jews gather motivates regular attendance at the synagogue and engagement with sacred texts.

lessons.title: Life After Death and the Messiah

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the Jewish concept of olam ha-ba?
A) The Garden of Eden at the beginning of creation
B) The world to come, involving continued existence after death
C) The Temple in Jerusalem
D) The weekly day of rest
practice_questions.marks: B) The world to come, involving continued existence after death [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Hebrew term used in Judaism for the Messiah.
practice_questions.marks: Moshiach [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two contrasting Jewish beliefs about the Messiah.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for each belief identified, 1 mark for each belief developed. Example: Orthodox Judaism believes in a personal moshiach, a specific individual descended from King David, who will rebuild the Temple and bring universal peace (2 marks). Reform Judaism reinterprets this as a messianic age — a time of justice and peace brought about through human effort and tikkun olam, rather than through one individual (2 marks).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Jewish beliefs about life after death.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed beliefs, each with a clear explanation and a named source. Sources might include: Maimonides' Thirteen Principles of Faith (thirteenth principle — belief in resurrection); the Talmud's description of olam ha-ba as closeness to God; the Tenakh (e.g. the prophets on a future age of restoration). Sub-tradition contrast adds depth: e.g. Orthodox belief in bodily resurrection vs Reform emphasis on spiritual immortality. Secure: Two beliefs addressed, source present but not fully developed. Developing: One belief developed; source named but not linked. Emerging: Basic points, no source, no development.

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in the coming of the Messiah is the most important Jewish belief.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Jewish teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Maimonides lists belief in the Messiah as his twelfth Principle of Faith, stating that one must wait for the Messiah even if he delays — indicating its centrality to Orthodox Jewish theology. The messianic hope runs through the entire Hebrew prophetic tradition (Isaiah, Ezekiel) and through daily Orthodox prayer. It provides hope and direction for the entire Jewish people. Arguments against: Judaism is primarily a way of life and action rather than a system of beliefs; observing the mitzvot, keeping Shabbat, upholding tikkun olam may be more central to Jewish identity than any particular theological doctrine. Reform and Liberal Jews re-interpret or de-emphasise the personal Messiah — yet they are fully committed Jews. The Shema's declaration of God's oneness might be argued as the single most important belief. Non-religious view: A humanist might argue that the concept of a Messiah is a human projection of the desire for a better world, and that the real work of repair is the responsibility of each individual, not a future leader. Justified conclusion required. Mastering: Balanced arguments for and against, Jewish sources on both sides, non-religious view included, justified conclusion present. Secure: Arguments both sides, source cited, conclusion present but not fully reasoned. Developing: One-sided; conclusion absent or weak. Emerging: Basic, listing, no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Daniel is a 13-year-old in an Orthodox Jewish community in Manchester. His grandfather has recently died, and the rabbi tells Daniel that his grandfather's soul is now in olam ha-ba. Give two reasons why this belief might bring comfort to Daniel's family.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct reason, up to 2. Acceptable answers: It teaches that death is not the end and that the grandfather's soul continues in closeness to God; it provides hope that righteous people are not lost but rewarded in the world to come; it connects to the belief in resurrection — that the family may one day be reunited.

lessons.title: The Covenant: Abraham, Moses and the Promised Land

before.content_html:
What Is a Covenant?

A covenant is not a simple contract. It is a solemn, binding relationship — in the Jewish context, an agreement between God and the Jewish people that carries profound obligations and promises on both sides. The covenants at the heart of Jewish theology are not merely ancient historical events; Jewish teaching holds that they remain active and binding today. They define who the Jewish people are in relation to God and what God expects of them.

Two covenants stand at the foundation of Jewish belief: the covenant with Abraham (recorded in Genesis 12 and 17) and the covenant at Sinai (recorded in Exodus 20), sealed through the giving of the Torah and the Ten Commandments.

The Covenant With Abraham

In Genesis 12:1-3, God calls Abraham to leave his homeland and travel to a land that God will show him. The promise is threefold: land (“the promised land”), descendants (a great nation), and blessing (through Abraham’s descendants, all the families of the earth will be blessed). This is one of the most important passages in the Tenakh because it establishes the special relationship between God and the Jewish people and holds out a universal vision — Abraham’s family becoming a source of blessing for the entire world.

The covenant with Abraham was renewed and developed in Genesis 17, where God gives Abraham the sign of Brit Milah (circumcision) as the physical mark of the covenant. Every Jewish male circumcised at eight days old carries the sign of this covenant in his body — making it an embodied, communal identity marker across all generations.

Key Fact

The Covenant with Abraham (Genesis 12:1-3) contains three promises: a land (Canaan, the “promised land”); descendants (a great nation); and blessing to all peoples of the earth through Abraham’s family. These promises form the bedrock of Jewish identity and hope.

Moses and the Covenant at Sinai

Moses is the most significant human figure in the Torah. After leading the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt, Moses ascended Mount Sinai and received God’s revelation. The covenant made at Sinai is qualitatively different from the covenant with Abraham: at Sinai, the entire Israelite people — not just one individual and his family — entered into a binding agreement with God. They would be God’s people; God would be their God. In return, they accepted the Torah and its commandments as their way of life.

The significance of Moses cannot be overstated. He is described in the Torah as the greatest of all prophets — the only person who spoke with God “face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Exodus 33:11). Jewish teaching holds that no prophet would arise in Israel greater than Moses, and his role as the transmitter of the Torah — both written and oral — makes him the founding teacher of the Jewish tradition.

The Ten Commandments

The Ten Commandments (Decalogue) recorded in Exodus 20:1-17 are the most prominent and widely recognised part of the Sinai revelation. They divide into two groups: the first four concern the relationship between humanity and God (no other gods; no idols; not taking God’s name in vain; keeping Shabbat holy), and the remaining six concern the relationship between people (honour your parents; do not murder; do not commit adultery; do not steal; do not give false witness; do not covet).

Jewish tradition teaches that the full covenant at Sinai involved not just the Ten Commandments but the complete Torah — 613 commandments covering every aspect of life. The Ten Commandments are understood as a summary or foundational statement rather than the entirety of divine law. In synagogue services, the Ten Commandments are recited on certain occasions, and many synagogues display them on plaques near the ark.

The Torah divides the 613 mitzvot into two broad categories. Mitzvot between man and God (bein adam l’Makom) include prayer, observing Shabbat and festivals, keeping dietary laws, and daily rituals of study and gratitude. These sanctify the individual’s relationship with the divine. Mitzvot between man and man (bein adam l’chavero) include not stealing, not lying, caring for the poor, and treating every person with dignity. These sanctify communal life. Jewish teaching holds that, for the mitzvot between man and man, God’s forgiveness on Yom Kippur cannot substitute for making direct amends to the person wronged.

The “promised land” (Eretz Yisrael) has remained a central element in Jewish consciousness throughout history, even during centuries of exile. Orthodox communities typically understand the promise of the land as literal and ongoing. Some Orthodox Jews make aliyah (immigration to Israel) as a religious act, fulfilling the covenant. Reform and Liberal communities hold more varied views: many affirm a spiritual or cultural connection to the land of Israel without prioritising physical settlement as a religious obligation. It is important to note that these are internal Jewish theological debates — the exam expects you to describe what different Jewish traditions teach, not to adjudicate the political dimensions.

Key Fact

Two foundational covenants: (1) Abraham — Genesis 12:1-3: land, descendants, blessing for all peoples. Sign: Brit Milah (circumcision). (2) Sinai — Exodus 20:1-17: the entire Israelite people accept God’s Torah and commandments; God becomes their God. Moses is the mediator. Together these covenants define Jewish identity and obligation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct reference for the Ten Commandments in the Torah?
A) Genesis 12:1-3
B) Deuteronomy 6:4
C) Exodus 20:1-17
D) Leviticus 19:18
practice_questions.marks: C) Exodus 20:1-17 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the prophet who received the Torah from God at Sinai.
practice_questions.marks: Moses [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two promises God made to Abraham in Genesis 12:1-3.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct promise, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers: a land (Canaan, the promised land); many descendants (a great nation); blessing for all the families of the earth.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the Covenant at Sinai is important in Jewish belief and practice.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons, each with explanation and development. At least one named source cited (Exodus 20:1-17; the Torah; the Ten Commandments). Sub-tradition contrast or application to daily life strengthens the answer. Example: 'The Covenant at Sinai is important because it gave the entire Jewish people a framework for living — the 613 mitzvot, including the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20:1-17, which means that every aspect of daily life becomes an act of obedience to God and a fulfilment of the covenant.' Secure: Both reasons present, source cited. Developing: One reason developed. Emerging: Basic points only.

practice_questions.text:
'The Covenant with Abraham is more important to Jewish belief than the Covenant at Sinai.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Jewish teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Abraham Covenant is the oldest and most foundational — it establishes the identity of the Jewish people as God's chosen people and promises them a land and a future (Genesis 12:1-3). Without Abraham there is no Sinai — the covenant with Abraham creates the people who will later receive the Torah. The physical sign of Brit Milah (circumcision) makes it an embodied, lifelong commitment. Arguments against: The Sinai covenant encompasses the whole people, not just one individual and his family; it gives the Jewish people their entire way of life through the Torah and the 613 mitzvot, including the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1-17). Jewish daily life is structured around the Sinai covenant — prayer, Shabbat, festivals, dietary laws all flow from it. Moses — the mediator of the Sinai covenant — is the greatest of all Jewish prophets. Non-religious view: A humanist might argue that neither covenant is literally true but that the ethical teachings they generated (justice, care for the poor, respect for life) are what matter. Justified conclusion required. Mastering: Balanced, developed arguments; sources on both sides; justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, source present, conclusion present but not fully reasoned. Developing: One side developed; weak conclusion. Emerging: Basic, listing, no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Levi is a 14-year-old at a Jewish school in north London. His teacher explains that the Ten Commandments are divided into two types. Explain two differences between the two types of commandment.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark per difference identified, 1 mark for each developed. Mitzvot between man and God (bein adam l'Makom) govern the individual's relationship with God — e.g. Shabbat, prayer, dietary laws — sanctifying the divine relationship (2 marks). Mitzvot between man and man (bein adam l'chavero) govern relationships with other people — e.g. not stealing, caring for the poor, honesty — sanctifying communal life (2 marks).

lessons.title: Moral Principles, Mitzvot and Pikuach Nefesh

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes Pikuach Nefesh?
A) A Jewish dietary law forbidding pork
B) The principle that saving a human life overrides almost all of the mitzvot
C) A festival celebrating the Exodus from Egypt
D) A form of daily prayer recited three times a day
practice_questions.marks: B) The principle that saving a human life overrides almost all of the mitzvot [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the Hebrew term for the Jewish concept of 'healing the world'.
practice_questions.marks: Tikkun olam [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which the principle of Pikuach Nefesh affects Jewish life in practice.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct example, up to 2 marks. Examples: a Jewish doctor or nurse may work on Shabbat to save a life; non-kosher food may be eaten if it is the only available way to survive; an ambulance driver who is Jewish will drive on Shabbat to reach an emergency. The rule applies across Orthodox, Reform and Liberal communities.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the concept of tzedakah is important in Jewish life.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons, each with clear explanation and a named source. Strong sources: Deuteronomy 16:20 ('Justice, justice shall you pursue'); Talmud Sanhedrin 37a; the teaching that tzedakah is rooted in tzedek (justice) not generosity. Sub-tradition application adds depth: e.g. how Reform synagogues organise food banks as a community mitzvah. Secure: Two reasons present, source cited but not fully developed. Developing: One reason developed, source named but not linked. Emerging: Basic points, no source.

practice_questions.text:
'Pikuach Nefesh is the most important moral principle in Judaism.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Jewish teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Pikuach Nefesh overrides almost every other mitzvah — if life is threatened, even Shabbat rules, dietary laws and festival restrictions may be set aside. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 37a) states that saving one life is equivalent to saving an entire world, indicating its supreme priority. It reflects the foundational belief that every person is created in tzelem Elohim (Genesis 1:27). Arguments against: Other principles such as tzedek (justice) and tikkun olam underpin the entire structure of Jewish social ethics and affect every interaction in daily life, not just emergency situations. One could argue that the Shema — declaring God's absolute oneness — is more foundational because it defines who God is, on which all other teachings rest. Some might argue that the covenant itself (the relationship between God and the Jewish people) is the most important moral framework. Non-religious view: A humanist might affirm Pikuach Nefesh's content (the supreme value of human life) while rejecting its religious basis. Justified conclusion required. Mastering: Balanced, developed; sources on both sides; non-religious view; justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides, source cited, conclusion. Developing: One side; weak conclusion. Emerging: Listing, no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Miriam is preparing a lesson for her synagogue youth group about why tzedakah is different from ordinary charity. Explain two ways Miriam might explain this difference.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark per point, 1 mark per development. Tzedakah comes from the Hebrew root tzedek (justice), not generosity — it means giving is a moral obligation, not a choice (2 marks). Because giving is obligatory, the recipient is not receiving a favour but receiving what they are owed by right of their humanity; this preserves their dignity (2 marks).

before.content_html:
Jewish Moral Principles: An Overview

Judaism is often described as a religion of action. Beliefs matter deeply, but what Jewish teaching emphasises above all else is how people treat one another and how they respond to God’s call to live justly. The mitzvot are not experienced by most Jews as burdensome restrictions but as a framework of sanctity — a way of bringing holiness into every moment of daily life. Jewish tradition teaches that no mitzvah is too small to matter: even feeding a hungry person or speaking honestly in a business deal is an act of worship.

Four core moral principles run through Jewish ethical teaching and appear explicitly in the Torah and the prophetic tradition: tzedek (justice), tikkun olam (healing the world), tzedakah (charity) and chesed (loving kindness). These four principles operate together and are reflected in countless practical mitzvot.

Tzedek: Justice

The Hebrew word tzedek means both “justice” and “righteousness.” The Torah commands, “Justice, justice shall you pursue” (Deuteronomy 16:20) — the double repetition of the word signals its urgency. Jewish courts (batei din) have a long tradition of applying Torah law to resolve disputes fairly. The prophets of the Tenakh — particularly Amos, Micah and Isaiah — repeatedly challenged the wealthy and powerful to treat the poor justly, warning that God is not satisfied with ritual worship when justice is absent from public life. “Let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (Amos 5:24).

Tzedakah: Charity as Obligation

Tzedakah is often translated as “charity” but the Hebrew root is tzedek (justice) — giving to the poor is understood not as an act of generosity but as an act of justice. The poor have a right to a portion of the community’s resources; the wealthy have an obligation to give. Many Jewish communities have a tzedakah box (pushke) in the home into which small amounts are placed regularly, making giving a habitual part of daily life. Organisations such as World Jewish Relief operate from this principle, providing aid to vulnerable people across the world regardless of religion.

A common error is to describe the 613 mitzvot as “rules Jews have to follow.” Jewish teaching frames the mitzvot very differently: they are not restrictions imposed from outside but a gift from God — a detailed guide to living a sanctified life. Observant Jews describe the sense of meaning and structure the mitzvot bring to daily life. Keeping Shabbat is not experienced as a ban on work; it is experienced as a weekly gift of rest and family togetherness. This is the texture the exam rewards: mitzvot as joyful duties and expressions of the covenant, not as arbitrary rules.

Tikkun Olam: Healing the World

The concept of tikkun olam — repair or healing of the world — has become one of the most widely cited principles of Jewish ethics in the modern period, particularly in Reform and Liberal communities. It expresses the idea that the world as it is is not as it should be: there is suffering, injustice and brokenness. Every act of justice, every act of tzedakah, every act of chesed is a stitch in the repair of the world. Modern Jewish organisations that campaign for human rights, environmental justice or refugee support often invoke tikkun olam as their motivating principle. Jewish Care and HIAS (the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society) are examples in Britain and internationally.

The Sanctity of Human Life and Pikuach Nefesh

One of the most distinctive and powerful teachings in Judaism is Pikuach Nefesh — the principle that preserving human life takes precedence over almost all of the commandments. The Talmud teaches that to save a single life is as if one has saved an entire world (Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 4:9). This remarkable teaching reflects the absolute sanctity of every human being, created in the image of God (tzelem Elohim).

In practice, Pikuach Nefesh means that if a life is at risk, a Jew is obligated to break Shabbat rules, eat non-kosher food, or disregard almost any other commandment in order to save that life. Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Jews all affirm this principle, though they may apply it differently in edge cases. Medical professionals in the Jewish community may work on Shabbat; an ambulance driver who is Jewish will drive to save a life. The principle shows that the mitzvot serve human life — they are never more important than life itself.

Key Fact

Pikuach Nefesh: preserving human life overrides almost all of the 613 mitzvot. Rooted in the teaching that every person is created in God’s image (tzelem Elohim) and that “one who saves a single life, it is as if they have saved an entire world” (Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 4:9). This principle is accepted across Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism.

Free Will and the Mitzvot

Jewish teaching holds that God gave human beings genuine free will. The mitzvot are binding obligations, but no one is compelled to observe them. The Torah presents the choice explicitly: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse; therefore choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19). The fact that God requires observance of the mitzvot but does not compel it makes every act of obedience or disobedience morally significant.

The tension between free will and divine commandment is one that Jewish thinkers have explored across the centuries. If God knows in advance what each person will choose, how is that choice truly free? Maimonides wrote that “free will is given to every human being” and that God’s foreknowledge does not remove human moral responsibility — a teaching maintained across Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism today.

Chesed — loving kindness — is expressed in countless ways in British Jewish community life. A large Reform synagogue in north-west London runs a weekly food bank and visits housebound elderly members; the young people’s group at a Manchester Reform synagogue organises clothing collections for asylum seekers. These acts are understood not simply as “volunteering” but as performing a mitzvah — fulfilling a divine commandment to show kindness to others. The distinction matters: chesed is not optional generosity but a religious obligation rooted in the covenant relationship with God.

Key Fact

The four core Jewish moral principles: Tzedek (justice — pursue fair treatment for all); Tikkun olam (repair the world — act to reduce suffering and injustice); Tzedakah (charity — giving as a moral obligation, not optional generosity); Chesed (loving kindness — showing compassion to all, especially the vulnerable).

flashcard_questions.a: Charity as a moral obligation, rooted in tzedek (justice); giving to the poor is what justice requires, not optional generosity.
flashcard_questions.q: What does tzedakah mean in Jewish teaching?

flashcard_questions.a: The preservation of human life; it overrides almost all of the 613 mitzvot when a life is at risk.
One who saves a single life, it is as if they have saved an entire world.
flashcard_questions.q: What does the Talmud (Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 4:9) teach about saving a life?

flashcard_questions.a: Justice — the requirement to treat all people fairly; 'Justice, justice shall you pursue' (Deuteronomy 16:20).
Loving kindness — showing compassion and generosity, especially to those who cannot repay it.
Repair of the world — the Jewish duty to reduce suffering and work towards a more just society.
Because they provide a framework for living a sanctified life, bringing holiness into every moment rather than restricting it.
flashcard_questions.q: Why are the mitzvot described as a 'gift' rather than a burden in Jewish teaching?

flashcard_questions.a: God gave humans free will, making observance of the mitzvot a genuine moral choice; this makes every act of obedience or kindness meaningful.
flashcard_questions.q: What is the relationship between free will and the mitzvot in Judaism?

flashcard_questions.a: A Jewish doctor or nurse may work on Shabbat if a patient's life depends on it, because saving a life takes precedence.
flashcard_questions.q: Give one practical example of Pikuach Nefesh in action.

flashcard_questions.a: By providing aid to vulnerable people worldwide, acting from the Jewish obligation to give rather than from voluntary generosity alone.
flashcard_questions.q: How does World Jewish Relief express the principle of tzedakah?
